A kibitzer is a person who watches what someone else is doing and then jumps in with their own opinions, advice, or comments — even though nobody asked them to.

The single most important thing to understand about a kibitzer is that their input is unsolicited. They weren't invited into the conversation. They weren't asked for their opinion. They just... gave it anyway. That uninvited quality is the heart and soul of this word.

The word is most at home around card games. Picture a group of friends sitting around a table playing poker. Now picture someone who is not playing — maybe they already lost, or they just wandered over — standing behind one of the players, leaning over their shoulder, and loudly whispering things like, "Oh, I wouldn't play that card if I were you," or "You should have bet more on that hand."

That person is the kibitzer.

They are not in the game. They have no stake in the outcome. But they can't seem to stop themselves from offering their two cents. The players find this annoying, distracting, and presumptuous — but the kibitzer rarely seems to notice or care.

The word stretched far beyond card games over time. Today, a kibitzer can be anyone who inserts themselves into a situation that isn't really theirs to be in:

  • Someone who watches two people argue and keeps offering opinions on who is right.
  • A coworker who leans over your desk while you're figuring something out and says, "You know what I would do? I would try it this way..."
  • A relative who watches you cook in the kitchen and constantly suggests you add more salt, turn down the heat, or stir differently.
  • Someone who stands behind a chess player during a match and starts muttering advice moves out loud.

In each case, the person has appointed themselves an unofficial advisor — an advisor that no one hired or wanted.
The Tone: Mildly Annoying, Rarely Malicious

A kibitzer is generally not a villain. The word doesn't carry the weight of something truly harmful. It describes someone who is more irritating than dangerous — an unwanted nuisance rather than an enemy.

Often, the kibitzer genuinely believes they are being helpful. They think they see something others are missing. They can't help but share it. This well-meaning-but-oblivious quality is part of what makes the word feel a little warm even as it describes an annoying behavior. You might sigh at a kibitzer. You'd roll your eyes. But you probably wouldn't hate them.

That said, the word is still a mild criticism. Calling someone a kibitzer is a gentle but clear way of saying: this person needs to mind their own business.

A kibitzer can also simply refer to a person who jokes around, chitchats idly, or banters — someone who lingers in a conversation mostly just to crack jokes and make small talk rather than to do anything useful. In this sense, the kibitzer isn't necessarily giving advice; they're just someone who hangs around and keeps the conversation lively (or drags it off course, depending on how you look at it).

This lighter meaning is less common than the "unsolicited advice" meaning, but you will encounter it, so it's worth knowing.
What Makes Someone a Kibitzer (The Checklist in Your Head)

When you encounter this word, three things are almost always true of the person being described:

  1. They are on the outside. They are not the main participant — they're an observer, a bystander, someone watching from the sidelines.
  2. They speak up anyway. Despite not being asked, they offer comments, advice, criticism, or suggestions.
  3. Their input wasn't wanted. The people doing the actual activity didn't invite this commentary and would be fine — actually, probably better off — without it.

If all three are true, you've got a kibitzer.
How It Differs From Similar Words

You might think of a kibitzer as similar to a busybody (someone who meddles in others' affairs) or a backseat driver (someone who gives unwanted instructions). The kibitzer overlaps with both, but it has its own personality:

  • A busybody is nosier and tends to get involved in other people's personal lives and secrets.
  • A backseat driver specifically gives instructions about how to do something.
  • A kibitzer is more passive — they're watching, commenting, opining — but not necessarily taking over or digging into your private life. They're more of an uninvited commentator than a true meddler.

Since you're learning the noun, it helps to know the word also works as a verb: to kibitz. If someone is kibitzing, they are doing exactly what a kibitzer does — watching and offering unsolicited opinions. The noun and the verb are essentially the same idea, just in different grammatical clothes.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever forget what "kibitzer" means, come back to this image: the guy who's not playing cards but won't stop telling you how to play yours. Everything else about the word flows from that picture.
